1. Too much CSS / inline CSS
Yes, you can overdo CSS—especially when using too many inline styles. It’s better to keep your styles in one place so it’s cleaner and easier to edit later.

2. Multiple CSS files
Yes, sometimes you’ll need more than one CSS file—like one for layout and another for colors or mobile design. It helps keep things organized and easier to manage.

3. Advanced websites using HTML/CSS/JS
Even big sites like Apple still use HTML, CSS, and JavaScript under the hood. They just use them in more advanced ways to make animations and layouts look high-end.

4. Limits of HTML
HTML only handles structure—it can’t really do styling or logic. That’s where CSS and JavaScript come in to make things look good and actually interact.

5. Unique perspective from the reading
I learned that web design isn’t just about making things pretty—it’s about structure, balance, and keeping code simple. Good layout and clean CSS make everything work smoother.

I’m working on my Senior Project right now, and we’re building the SOL Church App using React Native and TypeScript. We don’t use Node.js directly for the backend—our full stack uses Supabase for authentication, database, and storage. We connect to the DB through the Supabase client library, which handles queries and API calls for us. For development, we mainly use Expo, Supabase CLI, Docker, GitHub, and VS Code. All the skills from this class help us understand how web requests, state, and storage work when building our app.

While building our app, we learned a lot about how web requests, state management, and client-side storage work.

CSC 193A – Final Project

Option 2: Senior Project as Freelance Work
Student: Kanageshwaran Dhakshinamoorthy

Project Name: SOL Church App:
GitHub: https://github.com/Senior-Project-Team-Buildabyte/SOL-Church-App 
Introduction:

This document summarizes my work for the CSC 193A Final Project using my Senior Project, the SOL Church App, as my freelance web development example. It includes Jira proof, code snippets, UI screenshots, and descriptions of the features I built, such as Notification Preferences, the Image Slider click-through system, admin item availability, unit tests, and Docker setup. These tasks show how I applied web development concepts from this course to a real working project.

Jira Tasks (Proof of Participation):

Screenshots List: BB-150, BB-137, BB-132, BB-123, BB-118, BB-117, BB-100, BB-92, and BB-84.

Screenshot 1 – Jira Ticket: Connect Notification Preferences to Supabase (BB-118)

This Jira ticket documents my assignment to integrate the Notification Preferences feature with Supabase, including saving device tokens and updating user settings.









Screenshot 2 – Jira Ticket: Notification Service Unit Tests (BB-117)

This ticket shows the work I completed to write unit tests for the notification service to ensure correct behavior for token handling and notification routing. 

Screenshot 3 – Jira Ticket: Write Events Unit Tests (BB-100)

This assigned Jira task covers my work adding unit tests for the Events module to validate event loading, navigation, and filtering.

  

Screenshot 4 – Jira Ticket: Migration to Docker (BB-92)

This ticket shows my responsibility to migrate the project’s backend tooling and environment setup to Docker for consistent development across the team.

 
Screenshot 5 – Jira Ticket: Update Media Page Unit Tests (BB-150)

This screenshot shows my task to update and reorganize the unit tests for the Media Page, ensuring the new slider logic was properly covered
 
  
 
Screenshot 6 – Jira Ticket: Implement Click-Through on Image Slider (BB-137)

This ticket details my assignment to add internal and external link navigation when tapping images from the slider on the Media Page.

 
Screenshot 7 – Jira Ticket: Organize Tests Into Specific Folders (BB-132)

This screenshot shows my task to reorganize the test suite structure to improve clarity and scalability.

 

Screenshot 8 – Jira Ticket: Admin Can Mark Items as Unavailable (BB-123)

This ticket documents my work adding an admin feature that allows toggling item availability directly from the management screen.


Code & UI Screenshots:

Notification Preferences:

Screenshot – Supabase Fetch Code:

This code block displays a data-fetching function pattern used in the project. it demonstrates the general structure used when retrieving data from Supabase.
Screenshot – Notification Setup Code:

This screenshot shows the notification handler setup, including permission management, Expo token registration, and push notification configuration.

Screenshot – Notification Listener Logic:
This code screenshot shows how the app listens for both foreground and background notifications, enabling navigation when users tap an alert.

Screenshot – registerForPushAsync() Logic: 

This block shows the logic for requesting permissions and retrieving an Expo push token tied to the user's device.

Screenshot – savePushTokenToDB() Function


This screenshot highlights the function that sends a device’s push token and metadata to a Supabase Edge Function for storage.

Screenshot – updateUserIDForToken() Function

This code updates the stored push token with the user’s ID, allowing personalized notifications.

Screenshot – Notification Preferences UI

This screenshot shows the Notification Preferences screen UI where users can enable or disable categories of notifications.


Image Slider Click-Through:

Screenshot – Slider Fetch and Mapping Logic

This code block shows how slider images and their internal or external link references are retrieved and mapped for use in the front-end slider component.

Screenshot – Media Page Slider UI


This screenshot shows the Media Page UI with various event banners displayed in the image slider component.

Admin Item Availability:

Screenshot – Supabase Inventory Query

This screenshot shows the code that retrieves all inventory items, their categories, and availability flags from Supabase.

Screenshot – Filtering & Search Logic

This block shows how inventory items are filtered based on admin search input and whether unavailable items should be visible.

Screenshot – UI Data Mapping

This code maps raw database rows into formatted UI items for consistent display.

Screenshot – toggleAvailability() Function

This screenshot demonstrates the optimistic UI pattern used when toggling item availability. It updates the UI immediately, makes the Supabase update, and rolls back if the operation fails.


Screenshot – Admin Manage Items UI


This series of mobile screenshots shows the admin interface for viewing, filtering, and toggling availability of inventory items.

Unit Tests:
Screenshot – Jest Unit Test (Events Test)



This screenshot shows one of the unit test files for events, validating routing and data logic.

Docker Migration (BB-84)
Screenshot – Docker Compose Configuration

This screenshot shows the docker-compose.yml file used to orchestrate local environment services during development.

Screenshot – Terminal Logs During Docker Build

This block shows the Dockerfile used to define the project's runtime environment.


Screenshot – Docker Desktop Container View

This image shows multiple Docker containers running locally, including Supabase services and API instances.
This screenshot shows terminal output from building or running Docker containers for the project.

Reflection:

For my final project, I used my work from the SOL Church App Senior Project, where I completed key web-related tasks such as Notification Preferences, unit test suites, image slider functionality, and admin-facing item management. A major part of my contribution involved BB-117, where I connected the Notification Preferences feature to Supabase and synchronized user settings between AsyncStorage and the backend. I also implemented the click-through behavior on the Media Page image slider (BB-132), organized the entire test folder structure (BB-123), and added multiple unit tests for notifications and events (BB-100 and BB-92). Additionally, I contributed to project infrastructure with the Docker migration (BB-84), which helped streamline development setup across the team. These tasks allowed me to apply course concepts like state handling, API communication, routing, and organizing JavaScript/TypeScript code in a scalable way. Overall, the project helped me apply full-stack web development principles in a real production environment.
